subject: Consistent finishes across a commercial interior
hook: Look along a run of oak-effect doors. If the grain jumps direction, the eye catches it straight away.
ig:
Look along a run of oak-effect doors. If the grain jumps direction, the eye catches it straight away.

Wood-effect boards have a printed grain, just like the real thing has a natural one. Cut a door with the board turned the wrong way and the grain runs sideways next to its neighbours.

On a single kitchen cupboard, you might get away with it. On a reception desk front or a full-height office storage wall, it's obvious.

What good grain planning looks like:

- Every door and panel cut with the grain running the same way, usually vertical.
- Long horizontal pieces, like desk fronts, planned so the grain suits the piece.
- Panels labelled at the saw, so nothing gets swapped during assembly.

It's all decided on the cutting list before a board is touched.

Which would you notice first in an office: mismatched colours or grain going the wrong way? Tell us below.
fb:
Here's a detail that separates a good commercial job from an average one: grain direction.

Oak-effect and woodgrain boards have a grain pattern, and every door or panel can be cut with it running up or across. Get it wrong on a reception desk or a long storage wall and it looks patchy, even if the colour is perfect.

We plan grain direction on the cutting list before a single board is cut, so everything in the run flows the same way. Once you've seen it, you'll spot it everywhere. Have you noticed it before?
